item.title: DU hall provost resignation row sparks Chhatra Dal-Shibir clash
item.description:
A dispute over demands for the resignation of the provost of Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall at Dhaka University, following allegations of harassment by a resident student, escalated into a clash between activists of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) and Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir early Monday.
The altercation took place Sunday night as leaders and activists of the two organisations gathered outside the hall office amid tensions over students’ demands for action against the provost.
Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall Union General Secretary Md Emamul Hasan was injured in the incident, according to students.
The clash came hours after students, along with leaders of different hall unions and Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (Ducsu), confined the provost to his office and demanded his resignation.
The protest began around 9pm, when students locked the provost inside his office.
Ducsu Social Welfare Secretary AB Zubair and Literature and Culture Secretary Mussadiq Ali Ibne Mohammad, along with leaders of different hall unions, joined the protest. Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall Union Vice-President Abu Nayeem and General Secretary Emamul Hasan were also present.
The allegations were raised by Md Ibrahim, a student of the 2020-21 academic session in the Department of Robotics and Mechatronics Engineering, in a Facebook post on Sunday.
Ibrahim alleged that he was summoned to the provost’s office after sharing a social media post about problems at the hall. He claimed that his mobile phone was taken away, he was confined to the office and pressured to sign a written statement and keep the matter confidential.
The provost denied the allegations when contacted on Sunday.
As the protest continued, Shibir leaders from different residential halls gathered outside the hall office. JCD leaders and activists also gathered there, saying action should be taken against the provost following an investigation.
JCD leader and Bijoy Ekattor Hall unit Convener Thanbir Al Hadi Mayed alleged in a Facebook post that Shibir was trying to turn the students’ movement into a confrontation by bringing activists from different halls.
“Students had been protesting from the beginning, and JCD activists were also with them,” he wrote, alleging that Shibir was using Ducsu to bring activists from different halls and prepare for “another mob”.
Ducsu Literature and Culture Secretary Mussadiq Ali Ibn Mohammad, meanwhile, accused JCD activists of attacking students and said the hall union’s vice-president and general secretary were injured.
He questioned why student organisations were becoming involved in an issue that, according to him, should have been resolved through discussions between student representatives and the university administration.
A video circulated on social media showed Amar Ekushey Hall Union General Secretary Obaidur Rahman Hasib, also a Shibir leader, carrying several pairs of shoes in a small sack while entering Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall. Students later confronted him and questioned his presence there. The purpose of carrying the shoes could not be independently verified.
Ibrahim expressed concern that the JCD-Shibir dispute could overshadow his demand for justice.
He said students had initially demanded access to CCTV footage of the incident, but it had not been shown even after 2am.
“I am being deprived of justice because of this,” he said, alleging that both sides had brought people from other halls.
Around 3am, members of the proctorial team entered the hall and escorted the provost out of the hall office.
The university authorities have yet to announce any decision regarding the allegations against the provost.

item.title: India temple stampede kills seven
item.description:
A stampede at a Hindu temple in India’s eastern Bihar state killed at least seven people and injured 19 others on Monday, officials said.
Deadly stampedes are a common occurrence at big Indian gatherings and religious festivals, mainly due to poor crowd management.
The incident occurred at the Ashok Dham temple in Bihar state’s Lakhisarai district, where a massive crowd had gathered to pay homage to the Hindu deity Shiva.
The stampede was triggered after rumors spread that an electric pole had fallen on devotees inside the temple premises, district magistrate Shailendra Kumar told AFP.
“The situation is under control now,” Kumar said, confirming the casualties.
Around 19 others were undergoing hospital treatment, he added.
Bihar’s Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary called the incident “heart-wrenching” and announced compensation of 400,000 rupees ($4,180) to the family of each victim.
The tragedy is the latest in a series of fatal stampedes in India.
In November last year, nine people were killed in a crush at a temple in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.
Another stampede at a political rally in Tamil Nadu last year left 36 people dead.
One of the country’s worst recent crowd disasters occurred in 2024 in Uttar Pradesh, where 120 people were killed during a religious sermon attended by thousands of devotees.

item.title: DR Congo says Ebola outbreak now its deadliest ever
item.description:
An Ebola outbreak has now killed 2,325 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo, making it the country’s deadliest outbreak of the virus, according to government figures released Monday.
The United Nations says that the Ebola outbreak “is the fastest growing on record” and is killing a victim every 30 minutes in the DRC.
The deaths were from 4,945 confirmed cases, overtaking an outbreak in 2018-2020 that killed 2,299 people in the DRC from 3,381 confirmed cases.
The deadliest Ebola outbreak ever hit west Africa in 2013-2016, killing more than 11,300 people, mainly in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea.
The DRC outbreak began in the conflict-scarred northeastern province of Ituri and has since spread to five other provinces in the sprawling central African country of more than 100 million people.
Declared on May 15, it is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks at that point, and is the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
The World Health Organization last week said it hoped to reverse the spread of the disease in the country within three months.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

item.title: These everyday foods may be linked to higher cancer risk
item.description:
Diet and lifestyle choices can play a role in increasing the risk of cancer, although no single food alone causes the disease
Cancer risk is influenced by a range of factors, including diet and lifestyle. However, eating a particular food does not necessarily mean a person will develop cancer. Tobacco use, alcohol consumption, excess body weight, physical inactivity, and air pollution are among the factors that can increase the risk.
According to analyses by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), around 40% of new cancer cases worldwide are linked to preventable causes.
Research has also identified certain foods and substances that may contribute to cancer risk. Some contain or can produce carcinogenic compounds — substances capable of causing changes in cells that may lead to cancer.
Here are some foods and substances associated with increased cancer risk:
Processed meat and meat cooked at very high temperatures can produce potentially carcinogenic compounds.
Heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are chemical compounds that can form when meat or fish is exposed to high temperatures. These compounds are produced in greater amounts when meat is grilled, barbecued, charred, or fried.
Both HCAs and PAHs are considered carcinogenic, and exposure to them has been associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer.
Acrylamide can form when certain potato- and grain-based foods are fried, baked, or roasted at high temperatures. It can be found in foods such as French fries, potato chips, and some grain-based products.
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reported that high levels of acrylamide caused cancer in laboratory animals. However, it remains unclear to what extent the levels of acrylamide people consume through food increase cancer risk in humans.
Foods containing high levels of trans fats may also contribute to cancer risk. Fast foods such as chips, chanachur, shingara, piyaju, pizza, and burgers can contain significant amounts of unhealthy fats, depending on how they are prepared.
Trans fats can contribute to chronic inflammation and cellular damage. Some studies have also linked high trans fat intake with increased risks of colorectal, ovarian, and prostate cancers.
Tobacco remains one of the leading causes of cancer. Cigarettes, bidis, chewing tobacco, zarda, and gul contain numerous cancer-causing chemicals.
According to the WHO, tobacco can damage almost every organ in the body and increases the risk of cancer as well as several other serious diseases.
Alcohol consumption is also associated with an increased risk of several types of cancer.
Drinking alcohol has been linked to cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, esophagus, liver, colon, and rectum, as well as breast cancer.
When the body breaks down alcohol, it produces acetaldehyde, a chemical that can damage DNA and contribute to the development of cancer.
The use of pesticides in agriculture has raised concerns about exposure to certain chemicals. Some pesticides may contain heavy metals, organophosphates, and other compounds, and residues can remain on fruits and vegetables after treatment.
Long-term exposure to certain pesticides has been associated with health risks, although the relationship between pesticide residues in food and specific cancers can vary depending on the chemical and level of exposure.
Reducing cancer risk involves looking at overall lifestyle and dietary habits rather than focusing on eliminating a single food.
Avoiding tobacco and tobacco products, avoiding or limiting alcohol, maintaining a healthy weight, and engaging in regular physical activity can all help reduce risk.
A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, and other minimally processed foods is also recommended.
It is particularly useful to limit processed meat and avoid cooking meat for excessively long periods or allowing it to become heavily charred at very high temperatures.
Ultimately, reducing cancer risk is less about avoiding one particular food and more about maintaining a balanced diet, healthy weight, and active lifestyle over the long term.

item.title: Ronaldo says 'probably' in last year of career
item.description:
Cristiano Ronaldo believes this year is "probably" his last as a professional footballer, the 41-year-old Portuguese superstar said in an interview with Vogue magazine published on Sunday.
Ronaldo, who has established his place among football's all-time greats with more than 950 goals for club and country, had previously spoken of retiring "soon" or within "one or two years".
"This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy," he told Vogue, saying his future after football was "all mapped out".
"I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard," he said, listing travel and padel among his favourite activities.
"Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one," said the former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward.
Ronaldo married his longstanding partner Georgina Rodriguez in an intimate ceremony in the Portuguese resort of Cascais on Tuesday.
He told Vogue he wanted to "continue to enjoy what I've earned – what we've earned. Because after all it's been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice", referring to his glittering career.
After leading Portugal to the last 16 of his last World Cup this summer, Ronaldo is due to link up with his club Al Nassr for the new Saudi Pro League season.
